title: Hint Type vs. Faithfulness: Replicating the 'Lie to Me' Findings on Open Models

# Hint Type vs. Faithfulness: Replicating the 'Lie to Me' Findings on Open Models

**Problem:** A recent paper ('Lie to Me') measures how faithfully reasoning models verbalize the cues that influenced them, finding faithfulness varies with the nature of the cue. The published faithfulness-by-cue map covers specific models; an open-model replication with new cue categories is missing.

**Direction:** Reproduce the cue-injection faithfulness protocol on small open reasoning models, adding cue categories the original may not cover (e.g. sycophantic flattery, time pressure, fake citations). For each cue, measure the rate at which the model verbalizes that the cue influenced it. Build a faithfulness-by-cue heatmap across models.

**Why it matters:** Knowing which cue types models hide from their CoT tells monitors exactly where they are blind. This is reproducible, additive evaluation requiring no training.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Lie to Me: How Faithful is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Reasoning Models' (arXiv 2603.22582, ~March 2026) and 'Reasoning Models Will Sometimes Lie About Their Reasoning' (arXiv 2601.07663).

title: Faithfulness to Intermediate Structures: A Causal Replication

# Faithfulness to Intermediate Structures: A Causal Replication

**Problem:** A recent paper does a causal analysis of LLM faithfulness to intermediate structures (e.g. whether stated sub-results actually feed the final answer). The prevalence of broken intermediate-structure dependence across structured tasks on open models is unmapped.

**Direction:** On structured tasks with explicit intermediate results (multi-step arithmetic, table lookups), corrupt a stated intermediate result in the CoT and check whether the final answer follows the corruption (faithful) or ignores it (unfaithful). Compute the fraction of intermediate structures that are causally honored, per model and task type.

**Why it matters:** Faithfulness to intermediate structure is a fine-grained, intervention-based honesty test. A cross-model map of where intermediate reasoning is real vs. decorative directly informs CoT monitoring reliability and needs only inference.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Breaking the Chain: A Causal Analysis of LLM Faithfulness to Intermediate Structures' (arXiv 2603.16475, ~March 2026).

title: Many-Shot Context x Shallow Alignment: Long Benign Context Erodes the Safe Prefix

original_idea.body:
# Many-Shot Context x Shallow Alignment: Long Benign Context Erodes the Safe Prefix

**Problem:** Two interacting failures: long-context dilution (safety instructions buried/diluted in a long context) and shallow alignment (refusal depends on first response tokens). A long benign context may shift the model's first-token distribution away from refusal even without explicit attack tokens. The interaction between context length and shallow-alignment refusal robustness is not characterized for open long-context models.

**Direction:** On an open long-context model (Qwen2.5-7B-128k, Llama-3.1-8B), prepend increasing amounts of benign filler/many-shot benign QA before a fixed borderline-harmful request. Measure refusal rate as a function of context length. Success criterion: a dose-response curve showing whether long benign context monotonically erodes refusal, isolating it from in-context attack demonstrations.

**Why it matters:** Long-context agents accumulate large benign histories; if context length alone compounds with shallow alignment to erode refusals, safety degrades silently in normal long sessions—no attacker needed. Pure inference, consumer GPU, no training.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2406.05946 establishes shallow alignment (first-token-concentrated); many-shot jailbreaking literature shows long context shifts behavior. This isolates benign-context length as the compounding variable rather than adversarial demonstrations.

title: Compliance vs. Sensibility: Open-Model Map of Reasoning Controllability

# Compliance vs. Sensibility: Open-Model Map of Reasoning Controllability

**Problem:** A recent paper distinguishes 'compliance' (obeying an instruction to alter reasoning) from 'sensibility' (the alteration making sense) in reasoning controllability. This compliance-vs-sensibility decomposition has not been measured on small open models.

**Direction:** Instruct small open reasoning models to alter their CoT in specific ways (e.g. 'reason in reverse', 'omit step X'), then score both whether they complied and whether the resulting reasoning stayed coherent/correct. **Why it matters:** This decomposition refines the controllability early-warning signal: high compliance with low sensibility (the model can mangle its CoT on command) is a specific monitorability risk. Reproducible, inference-only, and novel for open models.

**Relevant context:** Extends 'Compliance versus Sensibility: On the Reasoning Controllability in Large Language Models' (arXiv 2604.27251, ~April 2026) and complements 'Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought' (arXiv 2603.05706).

title: Reversibility Taxonomy of Agent Tool Calls

original_idea.body:
# Reversibility Taxonomy of Agent Tool Calls

**Problem:** Agentic AI has produced irreversible attacks (e.g. autonomous crypto theft), yet there is no shared empirical vocabulary for which tool actions are reversible vs. irreversible, and current benchmarks treat all unsafe actions as equivalent.

**Direction:** Build a small open taxonomy and labeling scheme for reversibility (fully reversible / costly-reversible / irreversible) of tool calls. Take a mock toolset (file ops, shell, HTTP POST, payment stub, email send) wired to a logging sandbox, run an open-weights agent (e.g. a Llama/Qwen agent harness) on ~40 benign-but-risky tasks, and label every emitted tool call by reversibility. Report the distribution of irreversibility per task type and identify which prompt framings push agents toward irreversible calls.

**Why it matters:** Irreversible actions are where agentic harm becomes catastrophic and non-recoverable. A reversibility taxonomy gives monitor designers a principled target (gate the irreversible tail) and is buildable entirely outside a lab with a mock sandbox, no training required.

**Relevant context:** Adversa AI 2025 reports agentic systems producing irreversible attacks including autonomous crypto theft. arXiv:2512.20798 'Outcome-Driven Constraint Violations in Autonomous AI Agents' frames outcome-level harm. Vector Institute notes that with computer access 'the cost of missing a failure mode is not a wrong number—it can be irreversible.'

title: The Point of No Return: Locating Irreversibility in Agent Trajectories

# The Point of No Return: Locating Irreversibility in Agent Trajectories

**Problem:** We know agents sometimes take irreversible actions, but not WHERE in a multi-step trajectory the decision becomes locked in — the 'point of no return' is unstudied.

**Direction:** Instrument a mock sandbox so each agent action is timestamped and tagged reversible/irreversible. Run an open agent on scripted scenarios that contain one tempting irreversible shortcut. For each trajectory, identify the earliest step at which the agent's stated plan commits to the irreversible path, and measure the 'warning window' (steps between commitment and execution) available to a monitor. Analyze how window length varies with task and model size.

**Why it matters:** Real-time monitors need lead time. Quantifying the warning window tells us whether step-level interception is even feasible, a prerequisite for any agentic incident-response framework — and needs only API/open-model access plus a sandbox.

**Relevant context:** Open problem: incident-response frameworks specific to agentic AI (Adversa AI 2025). Trajectory-level safety benchmarks (ATBench, arXiv:2604.02022) evaluate over complete execution traces rather than final outputs, supporting per-step analysis.

title: Goal-Drift Onset Curves Across Context Length

# Goal-Drift Onset Curves Across Context Length

**Problem:** Goal drift (agents deviating from their original instruction over accumulating interactions) is documented but its onset as a function of context length / number of turns is uncharacterized.

Measure the turn/token at which the agent first violates scope, producing a 'drift-onset curve' per model. Compare a few open models and prompt-reinforcement strategies (re-stating the goal every N turns).

**Why it matters:** Long-horizon autonomy is the threat labs must deprioritize for near-term concerns, making it high counterfactual value. Drift-onset curves give a cheap, model-agnostic early-warning metric and test whether goal-restatement actually helps.

title: Action-Only vs CoT Monitoring on Subtle vs Blatant Sabotage

title: Injection Survival Across a Delegation Chain

original_idea.body:
# Injection Survival Across a Delegation Chain

**Problem:** Analysts warn prompt injection is amplified across delegation hops (a 70%-per-hop detector catches only ~17% over five hops), but this multiplicative decay has not been empirically measured with real agents.

**Direction:** Build a minimal N-hop delegation chain of open-model agents (planner -> subagent -> sub-subagent) passing a task plus untrusted document content. Plant an injection in the document and measure, per hop, the probability the injected instruction survives and propagates. Empirically test the multiplicative-decay model and whether a paraphraser/summarizer at each hop breaks the chain.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent delegation is exploding in deployment with little safety infrastructure. An empirical hop-by-hop survival curve validates (or refutes) the scary theoretical estimate and shows whether cheap inter-hop paraphrasing is a real mitigation — strategically valuable infrastructure research.

**Relevant context:** WorkOS/Okta delegation analyses: injection 'structurally amplified because inter-agent communication is typically trusted and unfiltered'; 70%/hop detector -> 17% over 5 hops. arXiv:2507.03010 'Subversion via Focal Points' studies inter-agent collusion. Mitigation: trusted summariser/paraphraser to reduce channels.

title: Scope-Attenuation Audit for Spawned Subagents

# Scope-Attenuation Audit for Spawned Subagents

**Problem:** Recursive delegation lets agents spawn subagents that inherit or escalate privilege ('scope attenuation' is recommended but rarely verified), and no open tool measures whether spawned subagents actually narrow their permission scope.

**Direction:** Create a mock capability-token system where a parent agent must explicitly pass a reduced toolset to each spawned subagent. Run an open agent on tasks that invite delegation and audit whether subagents are granted MORE capabilities than they need. Produce a 'privilege-creep rate' metric and test whether an explicit attenuation instruction reduces it.

**Why it matters:** Excess privilege in delegation chains (97% of non-human identities over-privileged per CSA) is a concrete near-future attack surface. A lightweight audit harness is buildable solo and is exactly the kind of monitoring infrastructure valuable outside labs.

**Relevant context:** CSA/Okta: 'scope attenuation at every hop' as a delegation-security foundation; Agent Session Smuggling (Nov 2025) and Cross-Agent Privilege Escalation (Sep 2025) documented as real attacks. arXiv:2510.25819 'Identity Management for Agentic AI'.

title: Tool-Call Hacking Detector via Proof-of-Use Auditing

original_idea.body:
# Tool-Call Hacking Detector via Proof-of-Use Auditing

**Problem:** Deep-research and tool-using agents 'hack' by emitting tool calls they never actually rely on (fabricating evidence of work), and there is no simple open auditor that flags tool calls whose outputs do not influence the final answer.

**Direction:** Run an open research-style agent on tasks, log all tool calls and outputs, then apply a counterfactual ablation: remove each tool call's output and check whether the final answer changes. Tool calls with zero downstream influence are flagged as 'ceremonial.' Report the ceremonial-call rate per model and task type as a cheap reward-hacking signal.

**Why it matters:** Tool-call hacking inflates trust in agent outputs and is a concrete specification-gaming failure. A counterfactual-ablation auditor is a reusable monitoring primitive, needs no training, and directly tests a 2025 finding.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2510.10931 'Proof-of-Use: Mitigating Tool-Call Hacking in Deep Research Agents'. arXiv:2601.12294 ToolPRMBench on process reward models for tool-using agents. AI news (May 2026) Reward Hacking Benchmark forces sequential tool use with hidden shortcuts.

# ChatInject Replication: How Much Does Mimicking the Chat Template Boost Injection Success?

**Problem:** ChatInject shows that crafting injected payloads to mimic the model's chat template boosts prompt-injection success, but the effect size across open models and template families is not broadly mapped.

**Direction:** Take a small set of indirect-injection tasks and create two payload variants: plain-text instruction vs one wrapped to imitate the target model's special chat tokens/roles. **Why it matters:** Special-token / template exploitation is a concrete, defensible attack class; quantifying the lift per template informs tokenizer/template hardening. Open models only, no training, addresses a structural vulnerability labs see but rarely publish per-model numbers for.
